text: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting in the gateway of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed with his face to the ground.

He said, "Please, my lords, turn aside to your servant's house. Spend the night and wash your feet, and you can rise early and go on your way." "No," they said, "we will spend the night in the square."
But he pressed them so strongly that they turned aside to him and came into his house. He prepared a feast for them, baked unleavened bread, and they ate.

versions.text: But he pressed them so strongly that they turned aside to him and came into his house. He prepared a meal for them, baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew מִשְׁתֶּה denotes a banquet or feast (literally a 'drinking-feast'), not merely a 'meal'. 'Feast' better conveys Lot's lavish hospitality and reads well aloud.

text: Before they lay down for the night, the men of the city surrounded the house—the men of Sodom, young and old, the whole population to the last man.

versions.text: Before they lay down, the men of the city—the men of Sodom, young and old, the whole population to the last man—surrounded the house.
versions.explanation: For oral reading the long appositional string delays the main verb too long. Placing 'surrounded the house' immediately after the subject keeps the sentence clear when heard, while retaining all the Hebrew detail.

text: They called out to Lot and said to him, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us so we can have our way with them."
Lot went out to them at the entrance, shutting the door behind him,
and said, "Please, my brothers, do not do such a wicked thing.

versions.text: and said, "Please, my brothers, do not do this evil.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb תָּרֵעוּ means 'act wickedly'; 'do this evil' introduces a definite object not in the text and sounds stilted. 'Do such a wicked thing' is both accurate and natural in speech.

text: Look, I have two daughters who have never been with a man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them whatever you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."

"Out of the way!" they said. And they said, "This fellow came here as a foreigner, and now he plays the judge! We will treat you worse than them." They pressed hard against the man, against Lot, and moved in to break down the door.
But the men reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.
Then they struck the men at the entrance of the house with blindness, small and great alike, so that they wore themselves out trying to find the doorway.
The men said to Lot, "Who else do you have here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters—anyone of yours in the city—get them out of this place,
because we are about to destroy it. The outcry against these people before the LORD is so great that the LORD has sent us to destroy it."

So Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who were pledged to marry his daughters. "Get up, leave this place," he said, "for the LORD is about to destroy the city!" But to his sons-in-law he seemed to be joking.
As dawn was breaking, the angels urged Lot on, saying, "Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, or you will be swept away in the punishment of the city."
When he hesitated, the men grasped his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters, for the LORD had mercy on him. They led them out and left them outside the city.
Once they had brought them out, one of them said, "Run for your life! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, or you will be swept away."
But Lot said to them, "Please, no, my lord!
Look, your servant has found favor in your eyes, and you have shown me great kindness in sparing my life. But I cannot flee to the hills, or the disaster will overtake me and I will die.

versions.text: Your servant has found favor in your eyes, and you have shown me great kindness in sparing my life. But I cannot flee to the hills; the disaster will overtake me, and I will die.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew פֶּן ('lest') expresses fear of a possible outcome, not a flat prediction; as it stands Lot appears to state the disaster will certainly overtake him. Also the opening הִנֵּה־נָא ('Look, please') has been dropped.

text: Look, there is a town near enough to reach, and it is small. Let me flee there—it is only a small place—and my life will be spared."
He said to him, "Very well, I grant you this request too: I will not overthrow the town you speak of.
Hurry, escape there, for I can do nothing until you arrive." That is why the town was called Zoar.
The sun had risen over the land when Lot came to Zoar.
Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah—from the LORD out of the heavens.

versions.text: Then the LORD rained down burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah—from the LORD out of the heavens.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two nouns joined by 'and' (גָּפְרִית וָאֵשׁ, 'sulfur and fire'). Collapsing them into 'burning sulfur' loses the explicit mention of fire, which is picked up in the imagery of smoke in verse 28.

text: He overthrew those cities and the entire valley, along with all who lived in the cities and everything growing from the ground.
But Lot's wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
Early the next morning Abraham went to the place where he had stood before the LORD.
He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and over all the land of the valley, and he saw smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace.
So when God destroyed the cities of the valley, he remembered Abraham and brought Lot out of the catastrophe that overthrew the cities where Lot had lived.
Lot went up from Zoar and settled in the hills with his two daughters, because he was afraid to stay in Zoar. He lived in a cave, he and his two daughters.
The older daughter said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to come to us as is the custom everywhere on earth.
Come, let us give our father wine to drink and lie with him, so we can preserve offspring through our father."
That night they gave their father wine to drink, and the older one went in and lay with her father. He was not aware of it when she lay down or when she got up.

The next day the older said to the younger, "Last night I lay with my father. Let us give him wine to drink again tonight, and you go in and lie with him, so we can preserve offspring through our father."
So that night also they gave their father wine to drink, and the younger one got up and lay with him. He was not aware of it when she lay down or when she got up.
So both of Lot's daughters became pregnant by their father.
The older gave birth to a son and named him Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to this day.

versions.text: The older gave birth to a son and named him Moab; he is the father of the Moabites of today.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew idiom עַד־הַיּוֹם means "to this day," a set phrase marking continuity from the narrative into the writer's present. "Of today" is a flatter, slightly awkward rendering and reads less naturally aloud.

text: The younger also gave birth to a son and named him Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the Ammonites to this day.

versions.text: The younger also gave birth to a son and named him Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the Ammonites of today.
versions.explanation: Same idiom as the previous verse: "to this day" better renders עַד־הַיּוֹם and keeps the parallel cadence between verses 37 and 38 for oral reading. A footnote noting that Ben-Ammi means "son of my people" could also help readers see the wordplay with "Ammonites."
